title: Israel and the Church
question: How do the biblical covenants fit together, and what is the relationship between ethnic Israel and the church of Jesus Christ?
intro:
Every reader of the Bible has to decide how the promises made to Abraham, Moses and David relate to the community gathered around Jesus. Are Israel and the church two stages of one people under one covenant of grace? Two distinct peoples with distinct promises? Or is the new covenant genuinely new, fulfilling and transforming everything before it?

The answer shapes how Christians read prophecy, apply the Mosaic law, baptize, and think about the modern Jewish people and the land. This entry sets out three families of answers at equal depth: covenant theology, dispensationalism (including its progressive form), and new covenant theology together with its close cousin progressive covenantalism.

positions.name: Covenant theology
positions.summary:
Covenant theology reads the whole Bible through a small number of overarching covenants. Most Reformed versions speak of a covenant of works made with Adam, broken in the fall, and a single covenant of grace announced in Gen 3:15 and administered in different ways under Abraham, Moses, David and finally Christ. Many add an eternal covenant of redemption between the Father and the Son.

On this view there is one people of God across both Testaments. Believing Israel was the church in its childhood; the church today is Israel come of age, with Gentiles grafted into the same olive tree. Promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ, the true Seed, and in all who are united to him by faith. Many covenant theologians nonetheless expect a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ from Rom 11.

figures.name: Johannes Cocceius
figures.profession: Professor of theology at Franeker and Leiden
figures.bio: German-born Reformed theologian whose federal theology traced redemptive history as a sequence of covenant administrations. His historical, progressive reading of Scripture was controversial among stricter Voetian Reformed colleagues but made the covenant a structuring principle for later Reformed thought.

figures.name: Herman Witsius
figures.profession: Dutch Reformed pastor and professor at Franeker, Utrecht and Leiden

works.author: Herman Witsius
works.title: De oeconomia foederum Dei cum hominibus (The Economy of the Covenants between God and Man)

figures.name: Westminster Assembly
figures.profession: Assembly of English and Scottish divines
figures.bio: Produced the Westminster Confession of Faith, whose chapter 7 gives the classic confessional statement: a covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace, one in substance but differently administered under law and gospel.

works.author: Westminster Assembly
works.title: Westminster Confession of Faith

figures.name: O. Palmer Robertson
figures.profession: Presbyterian Old Testament scholar
figures.bio: Twentieth-century defender who presented covenant theology as biblical theology, tracing a bond in blood sovereignly administered from creation to consummation, and arguing in a later work that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and the church.

works.author: O. Palmer Robertson
works.title: The Christ of the Covenants

positions.context: Covenant language was central to early Reformers such as Zwingli and Bullinger, partly in defending infant baptism against the Anabaptists by appeal to the continuity of circumcision and baptism. In the seventeenth century the scheme was systematized in the Netherlands, Britain and New England and written into the Westminster Standards. It remains the framework of confessional Presbyterian and Reformed churches and, in a modified form (1689 federalism), of many Reformed Baptists.
claims: There is one covenant of grace running from Gen 3:15 to the new covenant, one in substance though administered differently in each era.
There is one people of God in both Testaments; believing Gentiles are grafted into the same olive tree as believing Israel.
Christ is the true Seed of Abraham, so the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in him and in all who belong to him by faith.
The moral law summarized in the Ten Commandments continues as a rule of life, while ceremonial and civil laws have expired.
Covenant signs pass across administrations: circumcision and baptism signify the same realities, which grounds infant baptism in most forms of the view.

scriptures.reading: The first announcement of the covenant of grace: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent.
God promises to be God to Abraham and his offspring; the same promise is renewed in the new covenant and extended to believers' children.
One olive tree: natural branches broken off, wild branches grafted in. There is a single people, not two.
Paul identifies the singular Seed as Christ; the promises were always Christ-centered.
Those in Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise, so the church inherits Israel's promises in Christ.
Gentiles once excluded from the commonwealth of Israel are now fellow citizens in one new humanity, members of the one household.
The new covenant is the fullest administration of the covenant of grace, replacing the Mosaic administration that is becoming obsolete.

arguments.text: The New Testament repeatedly applies Israel's titles to the mixed Jewish-Gentile church: a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, the circumcision, the Israel of God.
Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised and uncircumcised alike, showing that justification by faith was the same in both Testaments.
If salvation in every era is by grace through faith in the promised Christ, then the people saved are one people, and the covenants must be phases of one gracious purpose.
The early church largely read the church as the continuation of true Israel, and the Reformed confessions of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries gave that reading formal shape.

critiques.text: Covenant theology imposes theological covenants (works, grace, redemption) that Scripture never names, and spiritualizes concrete promises about land, nation and throne, effectively transferring them from Israel to the church.

By stressing continuity it underplays the newness of the new covenant. Jer 31 promises that all covenant members will know the Lord, which does not fit a mixed covenant community including unregenerate infants.

responses.text: Covenant theologians reply that the categories are summaries of patterns Scripture does describe, much as Trinity is a summary term. Promises are not transferred away from Israel but fulfilled in Israel's Messiah, and through him to Jew and Gentile; many expect a future ingathering of Jews as Rom 11 indicates.

They argue that Jer 31 contrasts the mediated knowledge of the old order with direct access for all ranks under the new, not the visible church with the invisible. The New Testament still warns covenant members against falling away, so the visible new covenant community remains mixed.

strawMen.strawMan: Covenant theology teaches that God has rejected the Jewish people and that the church simply replaced them.
strawMen.correction: Classic covenant theology speaks of fulfillment and expansion, not rejection. Many of its major figures expected a future mass conversion of Jews, and believing Jews are full members of the one people of God.

strawMen.strawMan: Covenant theologians think Old Testament believers were saved by keeping the law.
strawMen.correction: The view insists the opposite: Old Testament believers were saved by grace through faith in the promised Redeemer, under the same covenant of grace as Christians.

positive: Gives a unified, Christ-centered reading of the whole canon.
Grounds a strong sense of continuity between Israel's worship and the church's.
Provides a coherent theology of the sacraments and of the family within the covenant.
negative: Critics argue it has sometimes fed supersessionist attitudes toward Jewish people.
Can flatten real discontinuities between Moses and Christ.
Its theological covenants are inferred rather than explicitly named, making it hard to persuade outsiders.

adherents: Many Reformed Baptists (in a modified 1689 form)

positions.name: Dispensationalism
positions.summary:
Dispensationalism holds that God has two distinct peoples with distinct (though related) purposes: Israel, an ethnic and national people with earthly promises of land, nation and Davidic kingdom, and the church, the body of Christ formed at Pentecost. History unfolds through a series of dispensations, stewardships in which God tests humanity under different arrangements.

Classic dispensationalists read prophecy with a consistently literal hermeneutic. Since God's promises to Israel were unconditional, they must be fulfilled to national Israel, most fully in a future millennial kingdom after the rapture of the church. Progressive dispensationalism, associated with Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock from the 1980s–90s, keeps the future for national Israel but sees the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated in Christ and the church as a genuine (not parenthetical) stage in the one plan of redemption.

figures.name: John Nelson Darby
figures.profession: Anglo-Irish clergyman, leader among the Plymouth Brethren
figures.bio: Left the Church of Ireland and became the leading teacher of the Brethren. From the late 1820s and 1830s, including the Powerscourt prophecy conferences, he taught a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and a pretribulational rapture. His travels in Europe and North America spread these ideas widely.

figures.name: C. I. Scofield
figures.profession: Congregational minister and Bible teacher
figures.bio: American lawyer turned pastor whose annotated reference Bible put dispensational notes beside the King James text. It became one of the most influential Bibles in twentieth-century American evangelicalism.

figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology at Dallas Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Gave classic dispensationalism its best-known academic defense, summarizing its sine qua non as the distinction between Israel and the church, a consistently literal hermeneutic, and the glory of God as the unifying purpose of history.

figures.name: Craig A. Blaising and Darrell L. Bock
figures.profession: Evangelical theologian and New Testament scholar
figures.bio: Leading voices of progressive dispensationalism, which emphasizes an already-inaugurated Davidic kingdom and a holistic, more continuous reading of the covenants while retaining a future for ethnic Israel.

works.author: Craig A. Blaising and Darrell L. Bock
works.title: Progressive Dispensationalism

positions.context: Dispensationalism arose amid early nineteenth-century British prophetic excitement after the French Revolution, in Brethren circles disillusioned with established churches. In America it spread through Bible and prophecy conferences (notably Niagara), the Scofield Bible, Bible institutes such as Moody, and Dallas Theological Seminary (founded 1924). It shaped fundamentalist and later evangelical eschatology and became a major theological source of Christian Zionism.
claims: Israel and the church are distinct peoples of God; the church began at Pentecost and is not simply Israel renewed.
God's covenants with Abraham and David include unconditional national and territorial promises that will be literally fulfilled to ethnic Israel.
Prophecy should be read with a consistent grammatical-historical (literal) hermeneutic unless the text signals figurative meaning.
History is structured by distinct dispensations or stewardships; the Mosaic law as a code is not binding on the church.
A future millennial kingdom will see Israel restored in the land under the Messiah (classic and most progressive dispensationalists).

scriptures.reading: God unilaterally covenants the land with specific borders to Abraham's offspring, an unconditional promise awaiting full fulfillment.
Israel will cease to be a nation before God only if the fixed order of sun and stars fails, guaranteeing a national future.
A partial hardening has come on Israel until the Gentile fullness; then all Israel, the ethnic nation, will be saved, for God's call is irrevocable.
Paul still speaks of the covenants and promises as belonging to his unbelieving kinsmen, implying they are not cancelled.
The church as one body of Jew and Gentile is a mystery not made known in earlier generations, so it is something new.
Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will be restored to Israel; he only declines to give the timing.
The Israel of God refers to believing Jews within the church, not to the church as a whole.

arguments.text: In the New Testament the word Israel almost always refers to ethnic Israel, and Paul distinguishes Jews, Greeks and the church of God.
If God's unconditional oath to national Israel could be reinterpreted to mean something else, the reliability of every divine promise, including those to the church, is called into question.

Premillennial expectation of an earthly kingdom is attested among second-century writers such as Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, so a literal reading of Israel's prophecies is not a modern novelty, even if the full dispensational system is.
Prophecies of Christ's first coming were fulfilled literally (Bethlehem, a virgin, a donkey), which sets an expectation that prophecies of his second coming and Israel's restoration will be too.

critiques.text: The New Testament itself reads Old Testament promises as fulfilled in Christ and the church; dispensationalism's two-people scheme divides what Paul says God has made one, and its literalism ignores how the apostles actually interpret prophecy.
Treating the land promise as an end in itself misses the typological trajectory by which the land points to the renewed creation; the New Testament widens the promise to the world.

responses.text: Progressive dispensationalists especially grant that Jew and Gentile are one in Christ in salvation, yet argue that unity does not erase ethnic and national identity, just as men and women are one in Christ without ceasing to be male and female. Acts 15 shows Gentiles added alongside a restored Israel, not replacing it.
Dispensationalists accept that the promise expands to the whole earth but deny that expansion cancels the original particular promise; a renewed earth can include a restored land for Israel.

strawMen.strawMan: Dispensationalists teach two ways of salvation, law for Israel and grace for the church.
strawMen.correction: Some early notes, including in the original Scofield Bible, were read that way, but Ryrie and later dispensationalists clearly affirm that salvation in every dispensation is by grace through faith; only the content of revelation differs.

strawMen.strawMan: Dispensationalism is just about rapture charts and unconditional support for the modern State of Israel.
strawMen.correction: It is primarily a hermeneutic and a reading of the covenants. Many dispensational scholars distinguish God's promises to ethnic Israel from endorsing any particular government's policies.

positive: Took Israel's specific promises and God's faithfulness to the Jewish people seriously.
Fueled Bible institute movements, lay Bible study and missionary zeal.
Helped many Christians repudiate replacement attitudes toward Jews.
negative: Popular forms have encouraged speculative date-setting and newspaper exegesis.
Critics argue it can sideline the Sermon on the Mount and kingdom ethics as not for the church.
Some forms foster uncritical political Christian Zionism, with consequences for Palestinian Christians.

Moody Bible Institute and many Bible colleges
Many independent Baptist, Bible and Pentecostal churches

positions.name: New covenant theology and progressive covenantalism
positions.summary:
New covenant theology (NCT) and progressive covenantalism are mediating positions that arose largely among Reformed Baptists. They reject the dispensational two-peoples scheme, affirming one people of God fulfilled in Christ, but they also reject covenant theology's single covenant of grace with multiple administrations. Instead they trace a series of biblical covenants (Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, new) that progressively unfold and reach their goal in the new covenant.

The new covenant is genuinely new: all its members are regenerate, the Spirit indwells every member, and the law of Christ rather than the Mosaic covenant as a whole is the believer's rule, with the Decalogue binding only as taken up and reinterpreted in Christ. Israel functions as a type of Christ, the true Israel; the church is not Israel renewed nor a parenthesis, but the eschatological people formed in him. Progressive covenantalism, articulated by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum, adds a stronger creation-covenant foundation and careful typological method.

figures.bio: Proposed progressive covenantalism, a biblical-theological reading of the covenants through detailed exegesis of the Hebrew covenant texts, arguing that each covenant advances God's kingdom purposes toward Christ and the new creation.

positions.context: NCT emerged among Reformed Baptists in the United States from the late 1970s and 1980s who held Calvinist soteriology but questioned the Westminster and 1689 handling of the law, the Sabbath and the covenant of grace. It gained academic weight when Gentry and Wellum published *Kingdom through Covenant* in 2012, which drew critical responses from both covenant theologians and dispensationalists and positioned progressive covenantalism as a third way.
claims: The biblical covenants are distinct but progressive; they should be read from Scripture's own storyline rather than through a single overarching covenant of grace.
The new covenant is new in nature, not only in administration: all its members know the Lord and have the Spirit.
Christ is the true Israel; Israel's identity, land and institutions are fulfilled typologically in him and, through him, in the church.
The Mosaic covenant as a whole has ended; believers live under the law of Christ, which includes the moral teaching of the Old Testament as fulfilled in him.
There is one people of God, but the church is the new-covenant community, not the old covenant people with Gentiles added.

scriptures.reading: The new covenant will not be like the Sinai covenant; every member will know the Lord, from least to greatest, and receive forgiveness.
Christ mediates a better covenant on better promises; calling it new makes the first obsolete.
The law was a guardian until Christ came; now that faith has come believers are no longer under that guardian.
Paul is not under the law of Moses but is under the law of Christ.
Jesus fulfills the Law and Prophets, so the Old Testament's authority for believers is mediated through his fulfilling work.
Christ abolished the law of commandments in ordinances to create one new man, signaling discontinuity with the Mosaic order.
The promises were spoken to the singular Seed; Christ is the true Israel through whom all promises are mediated.

arguments.text: Hebrews treats the old covenant as a whole, including its priesthood and law, as provisional and now superseded by a new covenant mediated by Christ.

If the new covenant guarantees regeneration and forgiveness to every member, then the covenant community cannot include members who lack those blessings, which bears directly on ecclesiology and baptism.
Typology escalates: the land, temple and kingdom find their antitype in Christ and the new creation rather than in either a mixed church or a restored national program.
The covenant of works and covenant of grace categories are seventeenth-century constructions; reading the covenants directly from the canon avoids importing later systems into the text.

critiques.text: NCT drives a wedge between the Testaments, weakens the abiding moral law (especially the Sabbath command), and risks antinomianism; its claim that the new covenant community is purely regenerate does not match New Testament warnings to professing believers.
Calling Christ the true Israel and reading land and nation typologically still empties specific promises to ethnic Israel; Rom 11 envisions a future for the nation, not merely a type fulfilled.

responses.text: Proponents answer that the law of Christ is more demanding, not less, and that nine of the ten commandments are repeated in apostolic teaching. Warning passages are means by which God preserves true members, not evidence that the covenant includes the unregenerate.

Many progressive covenantalists affirm a future salvation of many ethnic Jews from Rom 11. What they deny is that this requires a separate national program; Jews are saved into the one body by the same Messiah.

strawMen.strawMan: New covenant theology teaches that Christians have no moral law at all.
strawMen.correction: NCT holds that believers are under the law of Christ, which includes the moral teaching of the Old Testament as reaffirmed and deepened by Christ and the apostles. It rejects antinomianism.

strawMen.strawMan: Progressive covenantalism is just dispensationalism for Calvinists, or covenant theology for Baptists.
strawMen.correction: It shares one-people ecclesiology with covenant theology and covenantal discontinuity with dispensationalism, but its method of reading the covenants through escalating typology is distinctive to it.

positive: Encourages close exegesis of the individual biblical covenants.
Gives Reformed Baptists a coherent biblical-theological rationale for believers' baptism.
Brings fresh attention to typology and to the newness of the Spirit's work.
negative: Has caused friction within Reformed Baptist churches over the Sabbath and the 1689 Confession.
Critics find its view of the moral law underdefined.
Lacks a long confessional tradition, so its boundaries are still being worked out.

title: Baptism: Who, How and What It Does
question: Who should be baptized, by what mode, and what does baptism actually accomplish?
intro:
All Christian traditions baptize in water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, following Matt 28:19. They divide over three linked questions: whether infants of believers should be baptized or only those who profess faith; whether immersion is required or pouring and sprinkling suffice; and whether baptism is an instrument through which God regenerates and forgives, a sign and seal of the covenant, or a public act of obedience testifying to a salvation already received.

The earliest church order outside the New Testament, the Didache (chapter 7), prefers baptism in running water but permits other water and, if necessary, pouring water three times on the head, showing that mode was already flexible around AD 100. This entry presents three main positions at equal depth: credobaptism, covenantal paedobaptism, and baptismal regeneration (held in different forms by Catholics, the Orthodox and Lutherans).

positions.name: Believers' baptism (credobaptism)
positions.summary:
Credobaptists hold that baptism is for those who personally repent and profess faith in Christ. In every clear New Testament instance, people hear the gospel, believe, and then are baptized. Baptism is an ordinance commanded by Christ: a public confession of faith, a picture of union with Christ in his death, burial and resurrection, and the doorway into the visible fellowship of the local church.

Most credobaptists also hold that immersion is the proper mode, since the Greek baptizo commonly means to dip or plunge and since Rom 6 pictures burial and rising. Most deny that the water itself conveys regeneration, though some Baptist scholars (such as G. R. Beasley-Murray) argued for a richer, more sacramental understanding in which baptism is the moment where faith and grace meet. Churches of Christ combine believers' immersion with a strong link between baptism and the forgiveness of sins.

works.title: Believer's Baptism: Sign of the New Covenant in Christ

positions.context: Infant baptism was the near-universal practice of Western and Eastern Christianity by the early medieval period. The Reformation's appeal to Scripture alone led some radical reformers in Zurich to conclude that baptism should follow faith. They were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. English Baptists emerged from Puritan Separatism in the early seventeenth century, and by the early 1640s Particular Baptists had adopted immersion as the required mode. Today credobaptism is the practice of Baptists, Mennonites, most Pentecostals, many nondenominational evangelicals and the Churches of Christ.
claims: The New Testament pattern is preaching, repentance and faith, then baptism; there is no explicit example of an infant being baptized.
Baptism is a sign of the new covenant, whose members all know the Lord, so it belongs to those who give credible evidence of faith.
Baptism signifies union with Christ in death, burial and resurrection, best pictured by immersion.
Baptism does not itself regenerate; it is an act of obedience and confession by one already united to Christ by faith (with some credobaptists holding a stronger instrumental view).
The local church should be a gathered community of professing believers.

scriptures.reading: Disciples are made, then baptized and taught; baptism follows discipleship.
Those who received Peter's word were baptized; reception of the message precedes baptism.
The eunuch asks to be baptized after hearing the gospel; both go down into the water, suggesting immersion.
Buried with him through baptism into death and raised to newness of life, a picture of immersion and of conscious union with Christ.
Raised with him through faith; faith is the means of what baptism signifies, so it presupposes a believing subject.
Many Corinthians, hearing, believed and were baptized, the consistent order of the narrative.

arguments.text: Every explicit baptism in Acts is preceded by hearing, repentance or belief; household baptisms are each described with the household also hearing, believing or rejoicing.
If baptism signifies faith, repentance and union with Christ, applying it to someone incapable of faith empties the sign of its meaning or makes it a sign of something not yet present.
The earliest explicit reference to infant baptism comes around AD 200, and Tertullian then advises delay, suggesting the practice was not yet universal or unquestioned.
The new covenant differs from the old precisely in that its members are born of the Spirit rather than of the flesh, so physical descent no longer qualifies anyone for the covenant sign.

critiques.text: Credobaptism breaks the continuity of the covenant: children of believers received the covenant sign for two thousand years under Abraham, and nothing in the New Testament revokes their inclusion. It also makes baptism hinge on human assessment of a profession that can be mistaken.
Reducing baptism to a human testimony ignores passages that ascribe saving effects to baptism itself, such as washing away sins, rebirth of water and Spirit, and baptism now saving you.

responses.text: Credobaptists reply that the Abrahamic covenant had a physical and a spiritual seed; under the new covenant the covenant people are defined by faith, so the sign goes to the spiritual seed. Acts 2:39 adds 'as many as the Lord our God will call', limiting the promise to the called.

Those texts link baptism with forgiveness because in the New Testament baptism was the immediate expression of faith; 1 Pet 3:21 itself clarifies that it is not the removal of dirt but the appeal of a good conscience to God through the resurrection.

strawMen.strawMan: Baptists think baptism is just a symbol that does not matter much.
strawMen.correction: Baptists have historically suffered and died for believers' baptism. They call it an ordinance commanded by Christ, often require it for church membership, and many speak of real spiritual blessing in obedient participation.

strawMen.strawMan: Credobaptists believe children of Christians are outside God's care until they convert.
strawMen.correction: Credobaptists commonly dedicate children, teach them as part of the church's life, and many hold that those who die in infancy are saved; they simply deny that baptism should precede faith.

positive: Emphasizes personal faith and conscious discipleship.
Historically linked to the rise of religious liberty and the separation of church and state.
Encourages a regenerate, committed church membership.
negative: Can lead to repeated rebaptism of those who doubt their earlier profession.
Critics say it can individualize faith and weaken a sense of children's place in the church.
Requiring rebaptism has been a barrier to church unity with paedobaptist believers.

adherents: Baptists (Southern Baptist, Reformed Baptist, General Baptist and others)
Churches of Christ and Christian Churches

positions.name: Covenantal infant baptism (Reformed paedobaptism)
positions.summary:
Reformed and Presbyterian churches baptize both adult converts and the infant children of believing parents. The core argument is covenantal: God promised to be God to Abraham and his children, and gave circumcision as the sign and seal of that promise to infants. Baptism replaces circumcision as the sign of the same covenant of grace in its new administration, so the children of believers should still receive it.

Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of ingrafting into Christ, regeneration and forgiveness. It is not an automatic cause of regeneration, yet it is more than a human testimony: God uses it to confirm his promise, and its efficacy is tied to the Spirit's work in his own time and to the faith of the recipient. Mode is secondary; pouring and sprinkling are valid, though immersion is not forbidden.

figures.name: Huldrych Zwingli
figures.profession: Reformer and people's priest in Zurich
figures.bio: Zurich's reformer initially had doubts about infant baptism, but in controversy with the Anabaptists from 1525 he developed the argument from covenant continuity between circumcision and baptism that later Reformed theology inherited.

works.author: Huldrych Zwingli

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: Reformer and pastor in Geneva
figures.bio: Gave the classic Reformed defense of infant baptism in his Institutes, arguing that the covenant promise belongs to believers' children, that baptism and circumcision share the same inner reality, and that Christ's welcome of infants shows they can belong to his kingdom.

works.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion

figures.name: John Murray
figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology at Westminster Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Scottish-born Presbyterian theologian whose short treatise remains one of the most careful exegetical defenses of covenantal infant baptism and of pouring or sprinkling as valid modes.

works.author: John Murray
works.title: Christian Baptism

positions.context: Infant baptism was already the established practice when the Reformation began. The Reformed tradition retained it but needed a new rationale once baptismal regeneration was rejected. Facing Anabaptist challenges, Zwingli, Bullinger and Calvin grounded it in the unity of the covenant of grace. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Q. 74) and Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 28) codified this. The view is closely bound to covenant theology.
claims: The covenant of grace is one in substance in both Testaments, and the children of believers are included in it.
Baptism is the new covenant sign corresponding to circumcision; both signify cleansing from sin and union with God's people.
Since infants received the covenant sign under Abraham, and nothing revokes their inclusion, they should receive it now.
Baptism is a sign and seal of grace whose efficacy is not tied to the moment of administration, but is conferred by the Spirit to those to whom it belongs.
Mode is not essential: sprinkling, pouring and immersion are all valid.

scriptures.reading: God's covenant includes Abraham's offspring, and the sign is given to eight-day-old infants.
Paul links circumcision made without hands with baptism, showing baptism fills the role circumcision had.
Peter echoes Gen 17: the promise is for you and for your children, carrying the household principle into the new covenant.
Lydia and her household were baptized after only Lydia's faith is mentioned, consistent with household baptism.
Children of even one believing parent are called holy, set apart in a covenant sense.
Jesus welcomes children and says the kingdom belongs to such, so they are not excluded from its sign.
Circumcision was a seal of the righteousness of faith, yet it was given to infants, so a sign of faith can precede the recipient's faith.

arguments.text: Paul calls circumcision a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith, yet God commanded it for infants; therefore giving a faith-sign to infants is not incoherent.
Household baptisms (Lydia, the Philippian jailer, Stephanas) show the Old Testament principle of household inclusion continuing.
If the new covenant is a better covenant, it would be strange for it to be narrower than the old in excluding believers' children from the visible people of God.
Origen, Hippolytus's Apostolic Tradition and Cyprian attest infant baptism in the third century, and no early writer condemns it as an innovation.

critiques.text: The argument from circumcision assumes a continuity that the New Testament does not state; in Col 2 the circumcision without hands is spiritual regeneration, not a physical rite applied to infants. Household texts never mention infants and often mention the household believing.

Treating baptism as only a sign and seal detaches it from what the New Testament says it does. If baptism does not regenerate, the Reformed view struggles to explain why infants should receive a sign of what may never be theirs.

responses.text: Paedobaptists reply that Col 2 explicitly connects the inner circumcision with baptism as its outward counterpart, just as Old Testament circumcision of the flesh was meant to signify circumcision of the heart. The absence of any explicit command to stop including children is itself significant.

Reformed theology affirms that grace is truly offered and sealed in baptism, but holds that its efficacy belongs to the elect in God's time; this preserves both the objectivity of God's promise and the necessity of personal faith.

strawMen.strawMan: Presbyterians think baptizing a baby saves it.
strawMen.correction: Reformed confessions expressly deny that all who are baptized are regenerated, and that grace is so tied to baptism that no one can be saved without it.

strawMen.strawMan: Infant baptism is a leftover from Catholicism that the Reformers kept out of habit.
strawMen.correction: The Reformers re-examined the practice and gave it a new, exegetical covenantal rationale distinct from the Catholic one.

positive: Places children visibly within the church community and its nurture.
Highlights God's initiative and promise before human response.
Provides a strong theology of family and generational faithfulness.
negative: Can foster presumption that baptized children are Christians without personal faith.
In state-church settings it has merged civic and church membership.
Its middle position is criticized from both sides as unstable.

adherents: Many Anglicans (often with a different rationale)

positions.name: Baptismal regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran)
positions.summary:
For Catholics, Orthodox and Lutherans, baptism is a sacrament through which God himself acts: it washes away sin, gives new birth by water and the Spirit, unites the person to Christ and incorporates him or her into the church. Infants are baptized because they too need grace and because the gift does not depend on the recipient's prior understanding.

The traditions differ in emphasis. Catholic teaching speaks of baptism removing original sin and imprinting an indelible spiritual character. The Orthodox baptize by triple immersion and immediately chrismate and commune the infant, stressing illumination and participation in Christ's death and resurrection. Lutherans stress that baptism is water joined with God's word and promise, received by faith which God himself works, even in infants. All three insist that this is God's work, not human merit, and that the baptized must continue in faith.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop of Hippo in North Africa
figures.bio: In controversy with the Pelagians, Augustine argued that infant baptism, practiced for the remission of sins, demonstrates that infants inherit original sin and need grace. His view shaped Western teaching on baptism.

works.author: Augustine
works.title: On the Merits and Remission of Sins, and on the Baptism of Infants

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.profession: Reformer and professor at Wittenberg
figures.bio: Defended baptismal regeneration against both Rome's sacramental system and the Anabaptists, insisting that baptism's power rests in God's word joined to the water, and that infants can receive faith as a gift.

works.author: Martin Luther
works.title: Small Catechism
works.locator: Part 4, The Sacrament of Holy Baptism

works.author: Martin Luther
works.title: Large Catechism

figures.name: Alexander Schmemann
figures.profession: Orthodox priest and dean of St Vladimir's Seminary
figures.bio: Liturgical theologian whose study of the baptismal rite presented baptism as participation in Christ's death and resurrection and entrance into the life of the kingdom, recovering patristic emphases for modern readers.

works.author: Alexander Schmemann
works.title: Of Water and the Spirit: A Liturgical Study of Baptism

figures.name: Council of Trent
figures.profession: Ecumenical council of the Catholic Church
figures.bio: In its seventh session (1547) the council defined that baptism is necessary for salvation, that it remits original sin, and that infants are rightly baptized, against both Protestant and Anabaptist positions.

works.author: Council of Trent
works.title: Decree on the Sacraments, Canons on Baptism

positions.context: Baptism for the remission of sins is confessed in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381). Justin Martyr around 150 already calls baptism illumination and regeneration. As the church grew, infant baptism became the norm, and Augustine tied it to original sin. The medieval West refined sacramental theology; the Reformation split Lutherans, who kept baptismal regeneration, from Reformed and Anabaptist positions. The Orthodox have maintained the ancient pattern of triple immersion followed by chrismation and communion.
claims: Baptism is God's act through which sins are forgiven and new birth is given by water and the Spirit.
Baptism unites the person to Christ's death and resurrection and incorporates him or her into the church.
Infants should be baptized because they need grace and because grace is a gift that does not depend on the recipient's capacities.
Baptism is ordinarily necessary for salvation, though God is not bound by the sacraments (for example, baptism of desire and of blood in Catholic teaching).
The baptized must live out and grow in the grace received; baptismal grace can be resisted or abandoned.

scriptures.reading: Being born of water and the Spirit is the new birth given in baptism.
God saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, a clear reference to baptism.
Repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Baptism, corresponding to the flood, now saves you through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Ananias tells Paul to be baptized and wash away his sins.
Baptism actually unites us with Christ's death and resurrection, not only pictures it.
All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

arguments.text: The New Testament repeatedly attributes real effects to baptism: forgiveness, washing, new birth, union with Christ, salvation. A purely symbolic reading must explain away a large body of texts.

Second-century writers (Justin Martyr, *First Apology* 61; Irenaeus) speak of baptism as regeneration, and the Nicene Creed confesses one baptism for the remission of sins. There is no early alternative tradition of purely symbolic baptism.
If salvation is wholly God's gift, the clearest expression of that is the baptism of an infant, who contributes nothing and simply receives.
Jesus says the kingdom belongs to little children and that one must receive it as a child; infants are fit recipients of grace.

critiques.text: The New Testament attaches the effects of baptism to faith and repentance, which infants cannot exercise. Baptismal regeneration risks teaching that a ritual saves regardless of personal faith, contrary to justification by faith.
Many baptized people show no sign of new life, and the thief on the cross was saved without baptism. Scripture distinguishes the sign from the thing signified, as it did with circumcision.

responses.text: Lutherans especially insist that baptism is the very means by which God creates faith, so baptismal regeneration and justification by faith are not rivals. Catholics and Orthodox note that adult converts must believe, and infants are baptized into the faith of the church which they are then raised to profess.

These traditions agree that grace received can be resisted or lost through unbelief, which explains baptized people who fall away. God is free to save apart from baptism, as with the thief, but the church is bound to the means he commanded.

strawMen.strawMan: Catholics, Orthodox and Lutherans believe baptism works like magic and guarantees heaven.
strawMen.correction: All three teach that baptism works by God's promise and the Spirit, not by any power of the water as such, and that the baptized must continue in faith; final salvation is not guaranteed by the rite alone.

strawMen.strawMan: Baptismal regeneration means unbaptized people are all damned.
strawMen.correction: Catholic teaching recognizes baptism of desire and of blood and entrusts unbaptized infants to God's mercy; Lutherans hold that it is the contempt of baptism, not its lack, that condemns; Orthodox generally leave such cases to God.

positive: Offers strong assurance grounded in God's objective act.
Integrates children fully into the church's worship and life.
Preserves continuity with patristic sacramental theology.
negative: Can encourage nominal Christianity where baptism is treated as a cultural rite.
Historically justified coercive baptism and persecution of Anabaptists.
Critics argue it obscures the call to personal repentance and faith.

adherents: Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches
Churches of Christ hold a form of baptismal efficacy for believers only

critic.title: Believer's Baptism

critic.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion

readings.reading: Repentance comes before baptism; the promise to children is qualified by 'as many as the Lord calls', so it applies as they come to faith.
Peter echoes the Abrahamic formula: the covenant promise and its sign extend to believers' children.
Baptism is for the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit, and that gift is offered to children too.
The circumcision without hands is regeneration; baptism follows it and involves faith, so it is not simply infant circumcision's replacement.
Baptism corresponds to circumcision as the sign of the same covenant reality, supporting infant baptism.
In baptism we are actually buried and raised with Christ; it is the moment of spiritual circumcision.
Baptism saves as the believer's appeal or pledge of a good conscience, not by the water itself.
Baptism saves as the sign and seal of what Christ's resurrection accomplishes, received by faith.
The plain statement that baptism now saves you shows it is a means of saving grace.
The word is spoken to all in the house and the whole household believes and rejoices, so all baptized were believers.
The jailer believes and his household is baptized, illustrating household inclusion under the head's faith.
Baptism follows immediately at night, showing its urgency as the means of entering salvation.
The washing of regeneration is the Spirit's inner cleansing, which baptism pictures but does not cause.
The washing is the Spirit's work, signified and sealed by baptism.
The washing of regeneration is baptism itself, the instrument of the Spirit's renewal.
Burial and rising picture immersion and the believer's conscious union with Christ.
Baptism signifies union with Christ; burial language concerns spiritual reality rather than mode.
Baptism effects union with Christ's death and resurrection.

Swiss Anabaptists emerged from Zwingli's circle, and English Baptists from Reformed Puritanism.
Anabaptist challenge pushed Zwingli and Calvin to develop the covenantal argument for infant baptism.

argumentMap.text: Baptism should follow personal faith.
Every explicit baptism in Acts follows hearing and belief.
New covenant members all know the Lord.
The promise is to you and your children, echoing Abraham.
The verse limits the promise to as many as the Lord calls.
Baptism saves and washes away sins; it is not only a human confession.
Peter clarifies it saves as an appeal of a good conscience, not by washing the body.
Believers' children should receive the covenant sign.
Circumcision, a seal of faith, was given to infants.
Baptism takes the place of circumcision.
Whole households were baptized.
The household is also said to believe and rejoice; infants are never mentioned.
A sign without the reality leaves infant baptism without a clear purpose.
Baptism is the means by which God regenerates and forgives.
The washing of regeneration and birth of water and Spirit.
The early church universally spoke of baptism as regeneration.
The thief was saved without baptism; sign and reality can be separated.
God is free to save apart from the sacrament, but the church is bound to what he commanded.

title: The Lord's Supper: How Is Christ Present?
question: In what sense, if any, is Christ present in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, and what does the meal accomplish?
intro:
On the night he was betrayed Jesus took bread and said, This is my body, and took the cup and spoke of his blood of the covenant. Every Christian tradition repeats these words, yet they have divided the church more sharply than almost any other text. The question is not only what is means, but how Christ's risen body relates to bread and wine, whether the Supper is in any sense a sacrifice, and what believers receive.

This entry presents five positions at equal depth: Catholic transubstantiation, the Orthodox affirmation of a real change held as mystery, the Lutheran sacramental union, the Reformed doctrine of real spiritual presence (Calvin), and the memorial view associated with Zwingli. At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles and divided on this one.

positions.name: Transubstantiation (Roman Catholic)
positions.summary:
The Catholic Church teaches that at the consecration the whole substance of the bread becomes the substance of Christ's body and the whole substance of the wine becomes the substance of his blood, while the appearances (accidents) of bread and wine remain. This change is called transubstantiation. Christ is then present truly, really and substantially, body, blood, soul and divinity, and remains present as long as the appearances endure, which grounds Eucharistic adoration.

The Mass is also a sacrifice: not a new or repeated killing of Christ, but the one sacrifice of Calvary made sacramentally present and offered in an unbloody manner for the living and the dead. The vocabulary of substance and accidents draws on Aristotelian categories as used by Thomas Aquinas, though the Church holds that the dogma does not depend on any particular philosophy.

figures.name: Paschasius Radbertus
figures.profession: Benedictine monk and abbot of Corbie
figures.bio: Wrote the first full treatise on the Eucharist, arguing that the Eucharistic body is the same body born of Mary and crucified. His fellow monk Ratramnus replied with a more figurative account, starting the first major Eucharistic controversy.

figures.name: Thomas Aquinas
figures.profession: Dominican friar and theologian
figures.bio: Gave the classic scholastic account of transubstantiation, explaining how substance can change while accidents remain, and how Christ is present not as in a place but by way of substance.

works.title: Summa Theologiae

figures.profession: Ecumenical council of the Catholic Church
figures.bio: In its thirteenth session (1551) Trent declared transubstantiation a most fitting name for the change and anathematized its denial; in its twenty-second session (1562) it defined the sacrificial character of the Mass.

works.author: Council of Trent
works.title: Decree on the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist

positions.context: Early Christian writers such as Ignatius, Justin and Irenaeus speak of the Eucharist as Christ's flesh and blood without technical explanation. Debate in the ninth century (Paschasius versus Ratramnus) and the eleventh (Berengar of Tours, made to recant in 1059 and 1079) pushed the West toward precise definition. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 used the language of the bread and wine being transubstantiated. The term was then elaborated by scholastic theology and reaffirmed at Trent against the Reformers.
claims: At the consecration the substance of bread and wine becomes the substance of Christ's body and blood; only the appearances remain.
Christ is present whole and entire under each species and in every part.
The presence endures after the liturgy, so the consecrated host may be reserved and adored.
The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary and is offered as a propitiatory sacrifice.
Only a validly ordained priest can consecrate the Eucharist.

scriptures.reading: This is my body is to be taken literally; Jesus' word effects what it says.
Jesus insists on eating his flesh and drinking his blood as true food and drink, even when many disciples leave.
Eating unworthily makes one guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, which presupposes the body is truly there.
The cup and bread are a participation in Christ's blood and body.
A pure offering will be made among the nations in every place, read since the Didache as fulfilled in the Eucharist.
Do this in remembrance of me uses sacrificial memorial language (anamnesis), making present the event recalled.

arguments.text: Jesus' words of institution are simple and categorical, and in John 6 he lets disciples walk away rather than soften his language about eating his flesh.
Ignatius of Antioch calls the Eucharist the flesh of our Savior, and Justin Martyr says it is not common bread but the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus, showing realism from the second century.
If Christ is truly present in his body, something must happen to the bread; transubstantiation gives a coherent account of a real change without claiming any change in what the senses perceive.
Paul's warning about judgment for not discerning the body makes most sense if the body is objectively present regardless of the communicant's faith.

critiques.text: The Orthodox affirm the real change but criticize defining its mode with Aristotelian categories, which risks rationalizing a mystery and neglects the role of the epiclesis.
Scripture and Paul still call the element bread after consecration, so bread remains; and the sacrifice of the Mass detracts from Christ's once-for-all offering.
Christ's true human body ascended and is in heaven until his return, so it cannot be locally present on many altars; transubstantiation compromises the true humanity of Christ.
Jesus regularly spoke figuratively (I am the door, the vine); is in this context means signifies. Worshipping the host risks idolatry.

responses.text: Catholics reply that transubstantiation affirms what happens, not how, and that Trent deliberately used the term to safeguard the reality of change rather than to bind the Church to Aristotle. The Eastern Catholic churches retain the epiclesis.

Paul names it by its former appearance, as Scripture calls the angels at the tomb men. The Mass does not add to Calvary but re-presents the one sacrifice, as the Lamb in Revelation appears as slain yet living.
Christ is not present locally, as if moving from heaven, but sacramentally by way of substance; his glorified body is not limited as ordinary bodies are.

Figures like I am the door are obvious metaphors in context; at the Last Supper Jesus gives a covenant meal with no such signal, and John 6 pushes toward realism. Adoration is directed to Christ himself, not to bread.

strawMen.strawMan: Catholics believe they re-crucify Jesus at every Mass.
strawMen.correction: Catholic teaching states the Mass is the same sacrifice as Calvary made present in an unbloody manner, not a new or repeated killing.

strawMen.strawMan: Transubstantiation means the host would look like flesh under a microscope.
strawMen.correction: The doctrine explicitly says the physical appearances remain unchanged; the change is at the level of substance, not of chemistry.

positive: Fostered deep devotion and reverence for Christ in the Eucharist.
Grounded a rich tradition of Eucharistic theology, art and hymnody (for example Aquinas's hymns for Corpus Christi).
Keeps the sacramental and incarnational character of faith central.
negative: Became a primary point of division at the Reformation.
Medieval practice saw infrequent lay communion and the withholding of the cup.
Critics argue it fostered superstition and a priestly power over grace.

adherents: Eastern Catholic churches (with their own liturgical theology)

positions.name: Real change as mystery (Eastern Orthodox)
positions.summary:
Eastern Orthodoxy confesses that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, so that the faithful receive him for the remission of sins and life everlasting. Yet it has generally declined to define how the change happens. The Divine Liturgy places the consecration in the whole anaphora, climaxing in the epiclesis, the invocation of the Holy Spirit to change the gifts, rather than in the words of institution alone.

The Eucharist is understood as participation in the heavenly liturgy and the kingdom to come, the center of the church's life and of deification. Orthodox writers since John of Damascus have said that the Spirit effects the change as he overshadowed the Virgin, and that further explanation is beyond us. Some Orthodox documents of the seventeenth century (notably the Confession of Dositheus, 1672) used the term metousiosis, a Greek equivalent of transubstantiation, but many modern Orthodox theologians treat it as a borrowed term that should not be pressed philosophically.

figures.name: John of Damascus
figures.profession: Monk and theologian near Jerusalem
figures.bio: His summary of Orthodox faith teaches that the bread and wine are not a type of Christ's body but the deified body itself, changed by the Holy Spirit in a way that cannot be explained, just as the Incarnation cannot.

works.author: John of Damascus
works.title: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith

figures.name: Nicholas Cabasilas
figures.profession: Byzantine lay theologian and mystic
figures.bio: Wrote the classic Byzantine commentary on the liturgy, explaining the epiclesis as the moment the gifts are changed and presenting the Eucharist as the summit of the life in Christ.

works.title: A Commentary on the Divine Liturgy

figures.name: Alexander Schmemann
figures.profession: Orthodox priest and liturgical theologian
figures.bio: Argued that Western scholastic debates isolated the moment and mechanism of consecration, and called for recovering the Eucharist as the sacrament of the kingdom and the ascent of the church to the heavenly table.

works.author: Alexander Schmemann
works.title: The Eucharist: Sacrament of the Kingdom

positions.context: The Orthodox position grows from the Greek Fathers and the Byzantine liturgies of St John Chrysostom and St Basil. It was articulated against Byzantine iconoclasts, who called the Eucharist the only true image of Christ (John of Damascus and the Second Council of Nicaea, 787, replied that it is not an image but the body itself). Later, contacts with Latin and Protestant theology, including the Lutheran Tübingen theologians' correspondence with Patriarch Jeremias II (1570s–1581) and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), prompted more defined statements.
claims: The bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood.
The change is effected by the Holy Spirit through the prayer of the church, especially the epiclesis.
The manner of the change is a mystery that should not be defined in philosophical categories.
The Eucharist is a participation in the heavenly liturgy and a foretaste of the kingdom.
Communion is given to all the baptized faithful, including infants, in both kinds.

scriptures.reading: The bread Christ gives is his flesh for the life of the world; Communion is participation in divine life.
As the Spirit overshadowed Mary to form Christ's body, so the Spirit descends on the gifts to make them his body.
Communion (koinonia) in Christ's body and blood makes the many one body, the church.
Christ is made known in the breaking of bread; the Eucharist is an encounter with the risen Lord.
The words of institution are fulfilled within the whole prayer of the church, together with the invocation of the Spirit.
By sharing in the Eucharist believers become partakers of the divine nature.

arguments.text: The Greek Fathers and ancient liturgies affirm real change while rarely speculating on its mechanism; Orthodoxy claims to preserve this patristic restraint.
The Spirit is the agent of every new-creation act in Scripture, from creation to Incarnation to resurrection, which supports the epiclesis as the climax of consecration.
Since the Incarnation itself is beyond explanation, a sacrament that extends it should likewise be confessed rather than analyzed.
Paul's language of one bread and one body links the Eucharist directly to the unity of the church, a corporate rather than individualistic emphasis.

critiques.text: Refusing to define the change leaves the faith vulnerable to error; the Church has a duty to state clearly what happens, which is why Lateran IV and Trent did so. Locating consecration in the epiclesis rather than the words of Christ is also questioned.
A real change of the elements is not taught in Scripture, which still calls them bread and wine; the union is sacramental, not a conversion.
A bodily change in the elements conflicts with Christ's ascended humanity; it is the believer who is lifted to Christ by the Spirit, not the elements changed.
Appealing to mystery cannot rescue a doctrine that lacks clear scriptural basis; the Supper is a remembrance, and the Spirit dwells in believers, not in bread.

responses.text: The Orthodox reply that the church's dogmatic tradition defines only what is necessary; the whole anaphora consecrates, and the Latin rite itself once had an epiclesis. Precision about mechanism is not the same as fidelity to the mystery.
Scripture calls the elements bread because that is how they appear and are eaten, but Christ calls them his body; the change is real, as John of Damascus taught.

The ascension does not imprison Christ in a place; his glorified humanity, united to his divinity, can be present where he wills. Orthodoxy also speaks of the church being lifted up, holding both together.
Remembrance in biblical usage is participation, as Israel's Passover made the exodus present. The early church received the Eucharist as Christ's body before any New Testament canon was settled.

strawMen.strawMan: The Orthodox view is just transubstantiation in Greek.
strawMen.correction: The Orthodox share the belief in real change but resist scholastic categories, emphasize the epiclesis, and frame the Eucharist liturgically and eschatologically. Some Orthodox texts used metousiosis, but this is not a dogmatic commitment to Aristotelian metaphysics.

strawMen.strawMan: Calling it a mystery means the Orthodox have no clear belief.
strawMen.correction: They have a clear belief that the gifts truly become Christ's body and blood; mystery refers to the manner, not the reality.

positive: Keeps the Eucharist at the heart of a richly theological liturgy.
Holds together the Spirit's work, the church and the kingdom in sacramental theology.
Infant communion integrates children fully into the eucharistic life.
negative: In practice frequent communion declined for centuries in many Orthodox lands.
Critics see the appeal to mystery as evading necessary questions.
Closed communion keeps sharp boundaries with other churches.

adherents: Some Anglican and ecumenical liturgical scholars

positions.name: Sacramental union (Lutheran)
positions.summary:
Lutherans confess that in the Lord's Supper the true body and blood of Christ are truly and substantially present in, with and under the bread and wine, and are distributed and received by all who eat and drink, whether believing or not. The bread remains bread and the wine remains wine, yet by Christ's word they are united with his body and blood in a sacramental union. Lutherans insist this is not consubstantiation in the sense of a physical mixture or local enclosure, a label they usually reject.

The Supper is not a sacrifice we offer but a gift Christ gives: his body and blood for the forgiveness of sins, received with benefit by faith. Unworthy communicants receive the body too, but to their judgment (the oral eating and the eating of the unworthy). The possibility of the body's presence is grounded in the personal union of Christ's two natures, by which his humanity shares divine attributes, including presence wherever he wills.

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.profession: Reformer and professor at Wittenberg
figures.bio: Rejected transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass in 1520, but fought Zwingli and Oecolampadius over the real presence, insisting on the plain words This is my body. At Marburg he reportedly wrote those words on the table.

figures.profession: Lutheran church historian in Germany and Australia
figures.bio: Wrote a major historical and theological study of the Marburg controversy that defended the Lutheran confession of the real presence in the twentieth century.

works.author: Hermann Sasse
works.title: This Is My Body: Luther's Contention for the Real Presence in the Sacrament of the Altar

positions.context: Luther's 1520 *Babylonian Captivity* attacked transubstantiation and the Mass as sacrifice but kept the real presence. From 1524 Karlstadt, Zwingli and Oecolampadius argued for a figurative reading, leading to bitter pamphlet exchanges and the failed Marburg Colloquy (1529). The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article X) and Formula of Concord (1577, Article VII) codified the Lutheran view, which separated Lutherans from Reformed churches until twentieth-century agreements such as the Leuenberg Agreement (1973), which not all Lutherans accept.
claims: Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine.
The bread and wine remain; there is a sacramental union, not a change of substance.
All communicants receive Christ's body and blood orally, the faithful for blessing and the unworthy for judgment.
The Supper is God's gift of forgiveness, not a sacrifice offered by the church.
Christ's human nature, by the personal union, can be present wherever he has promised to be.

scriptures.reading: This is my body and my blood for the forgiveness of sins must be taken at face value; Christ's word does not lie.
The bread we break is a participation (koinonia) in the body of Christ: bread and body together.
The unworthy are guilty of the body and blood, proving that even unbelievers receive them.
Given for you, shed for you: the Supper delivers the fruits of the cross as a gift.
Christ ascended far above the heavens to fill all things, so his ascension is not confinement to a place.
Christ promises his presence always; the Supper is where he has specifically bound that promise.

arguments.text: The words of institution are clear and contain no hint of metaphor; when God's word speaks plainly, faith submits even when reason objects.
Paul says unworthy eaters sin against the body and blood, which implies the body is present for all who eat, not only for the faithful.
If Christ's humanity and divinity are one person, his humanity cannot be absent where his divinity is present; locating his body only in heaven separates the natures.

The ancient church affirmed bread and body together (Irenaeus speaks of the Eucharist as consisting of an earthly and a heavenly reality), which fits sacramental union better than conversion or symbol.

critiques.text: If Christ's word says this is my body, saying it remains bread too qualifies Christ's word; the Lutheran view, rejected by Trent, is unstable.
Lutheran Christology of ubiquity is a speculative scheme of its own, and the Lutherans' rejection of the Eucharist as sacrifice departs from the patristic liturgy.

Ubiquity of Christ's human body confuses the natures and makes his body unlike ours, undermining the true humanity he shares with us; Scripture says heaven must receive him until the restoration of all things.
Luther's literalism is selective; he does not take the cup is the new covenant literally. John 6 says the flesh profits nothing.

responses.text: Lutherans answer that Paul himself calls the consecrated element bread, so affirming both is biblical; the union of bread and body parallels the union of two natures in Christ without either being destroyed.

The Formula of Concord grounds the presence in Christ's promise rather than a general ubiquity; and the Lutheran liturgy retains thanksgiving and offering of praise while denying a propitiatory sacrifice.
The right hand of God is not a place but God's power and rule; Christ's humanity, exalted there, can be present where he wills without ceasing to be human.

The cup is the new covenant by metonymy because it contains the covenant blood; John 6:63 contrasts flesh as fallen human nature with the Spirit, not Christ's own flesh, which John 6:51 calls life for the world.

strawMen.strawMan: Lutherans believe in consubstantiation, a mixing of two substances into one.
strawMen.correction: The Lutheran confessions do not use the term and most Lutherans reject it as implying a physical mixture; they speak of a sacramental union effected by Christ's word.

strawMen.strawMan: Luther's view is just a halfway house between Rome and Zwingli.
strawMen.correction: Luther's view is a distinct position resting on Christology and the authority of the plain word; he rejected Rome's sacrifice and transubstantiation as firmly as he rejected Zwingli's symbolism.

positive: Preserved a strong sense of the Supper as gift and assurance of forgiveness.
Grounded rich Lutheran sacramental piety and music, for example the Bach cantata tradition.
Kept Christology and sacraments tightly connected.
negative: The Marburg split permanently divided Protestantism politically and confessionally.
Ubiquity debates became highly technical.
Closed communion in some Lutheran bodies remains a barrier to fellowship.

adherents: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod and other confessional Lutheran churches

positions.name: Real spiritual presence (Reformed, Calvin)
positions.summary:
Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that in the Supper believers truly feed on the body and blood of Christ, not merely recalling him. Yet Christ's body remains in heaven at the Father's right hand. The bridge is the Holy Spirit, who unites believers to the whole Christ and lifts them up (sursum corda, lift up your hearts) to commune with him. The bread and wine are not changed or joined to the body but are signs and seals by which God truly gives what they signify.

The presence is real but spiritual, meaning effected by the Spirit, not meaning less real. It is received by faith: unbelievers receive only the outward signs, to their condemnation for despising the gift. The Supper nourishes union with Christ, strengthens faith, and binds the church together.

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: Reformer and pastor in Geneva
figures.bio: Sought a middle path between Luther and Zwingli, affirming true communion with the substance of Christ's flesh through the Spirit while denying local presence. He confessed the mystery to be greater than he could express.

figures.name: Heinrich Bullinger
figures.profession: Zwingli's successor in Zurich
figures.bio: Negotiated the Consensus Tigurinus (1549) with Calvin, uniting the Zurich and Geneva churches on the Supper; later authored the Second Helvetic Confession (1566).

figures.name: John Williamson Nevin
figures.profession: German Reformed theologian at Mercersburg Seminary
figures.bio: Argued that American Reformed churches had drifted into memorialism and called them back to Calvin's high view, provoking a sharp exchange with Charles Hodge of Princeton.

works.author: John Williamson Nevin
works.title: The Mystical Presence

positions.context: Calvin came to prominence after Marburg, trying to heal the Protestant split. The Consensus Tigurinus (1549) brought Zurich and Geneva together, but provoked Lutheran critics such as Joachim Westphal, deepening the Lutheran-Reformed divide. The view entered the Belgic Confession (1561, Art. 35), the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, QQ. 75-80), the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571, Art. 28 in its Anglican form) and the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 29).
claims: Believers truly partake of Christ's body and blood, not merely recall him.
Christ's human body is in heaven and is not locally present in or with the elements.
The Holy Spirit unites believers to Christ and lifts them to commune with him.
The elements are signs and seals that truly convey what they signify to faith.
Unbelievers receive only the signs, not Christ, and eat to their judgment.

scriptures.reading: Participation in Christ's body and blood is real communion with him, effected by the Spirit.
It is the Spirit who gives life; Christ's flesh nourishes us by the Spirit, not by physical eating.
Heaven must receive Christ until the restoration of all things, so his body is not on earth.
Believers seek things above, where Christ is seated; in the Supper hearts are lifted up to him.
By one Spirit we are baptized into one body and made to drink of one Spirit; the Spirit is the bond of union.
Union with Christ is a great mystery; the Supper nourishes this real union.

arguments.text: The New Testament locates Christ's body in heaven until his return, while also promising real communion with him; only a Spirit-mediated presence honors both.
A true human body has location and extension; to make it present in many places at once denies the reality of Christ's humanity, which is essential to our salvation.
Sacramental language in Scripture regularly calls a sign by the name of the thing signified (circumcision is called the covenant, the rock was Christ), so this is my body is sacramental speech.
Augustine's distinction between sign (sacramentum) and reality (res), and his teaching that the wicked receive the sacrament but not its power, anticipates Calvin's position.

critiques.text: A spiritual presence dependent on the communicant's faith weakens the objective reality Christ's words establish; Paul's warning about the body applies to all.
Calvin's spatial reasoning about Christ's body imposes a modern physics on a mystery; the epiclesis brings the Spirit upon the gifts themselves, not only on the communicants.
Calvin's view makes faith, not Christ's word, the decisive factor and so removes the true body from the Supper; ultimately it is Zwinglian in a different vocabulary.
Talk of feeding on the substance of Christ's flesh through the Spirit is unclear and unnecessary; communion with Christ by faith happens at all times, so nothing unique occurs at the table.

responses.text: Christ is truly offered to all who come, so the gift is objective; but a gift offered is received only by faith, as the gospel itself is.

The Reformed confessions also invoke the Spirit and confess mystery; Calvin said he would rather experience it than understand it. They simply hold that the ascension is part of the revealed data, not modern physics.
Calvin affirmed true feeding on Christ's flesh and blood, which Zwingli did not; the Spirit, not faith, effects the union, and faith is the hand that receives.
Communion with Christ is not confined to the table, but God has appointed the Supper as a particular means by which he strengthens that union, just as preaching is a particular means of grace.

strawMen.strawMan: Calvin's spiritual presence means the presence is imaginary or only in the mind.
strawMen.correction: Calvin insisted believers truly receive Christ's body and blood; spiritual means by the Holy Spirit, not unreal or merely mental.

strawMen.strawMan: The Reformed view is the same as Zwingli's memorialism.
strawMen.correction: Calvin explicitly criticized views that made the Supper merely a memorial, and Reformed confessions speak of real feeding on Christ.

positive: Offers a mediating position that unified Swiss Protestantism.
Connects the Supper to union with Christ and the work of the Spirit.
Avoids both local presence and bare symbolism.
negative: Satisfied neither Lutherans nor memorialists and has often drifted toward memorialism in practice.
Its spatial language about heaven raises questions for some theologians.
Infrequent communion in many Reformed churches belied Calvin's wish for weekly celebration.

adherents: Mercersburg theology and its modern heirs

positions.name: Memorial view (Zwinglian)
positions.summary:
The memorial view holds that the bread and wine are signs that represent Christ's body and blood. In the words This is my body, the verb is means signifies, as in many biblical figures of speech. Christ's body is in heaven, and the benefit of the Supper is the believing remembrance of his death, thanksgiving, proclamation and the fellowship of the church.

Zwingli himself held more than a bare symbol: he spoke of Christ being present to the contemplation of faith and of the congregation becoming his body as it gathers. Later memorialists, especially Baptists and many evangelicals, emphasize the Supper as an act of obedience, remembrance, self-examination, covenant renewal and anticipation of his return, without any special presence in the elements.

positions.context: Late medieval critiques of eucharistic practice, Erasmian humanism and Hoen's letter (circulating c. 1521–1524) prepared the way. Zwingli developed the view in Zurich from 1524–1525, and debated Luther at the Marburg Colloquy (October 1529), which agreed on fourteen articles but not on the presence. After Zwingli's death, Bullinger moved closer to Calvin. The memorial view later became widespread among Anabaptists, Baptists, revivalist and many nondenominational evangelical churches.
claims: The bread and wine are signs representing Christ's body and blood; they are not changed or united to them.
The words This is my body are figurative, with is meaning signifies.
Christ's body is in heaven; he is present by his Spirit and divinity to faith, not bodily in the elements.
The Supper is a memorial of Christ's death, a proclamation, thanksgiving and fellowship meal of the church.
Its benefit comes through faith, remembrance and obedience, not through the elements themselves.

scriptures.reading: Do this in remembrance of me defines the purpose of the Supper as remembrance.
Eating and drinking proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, an act of proclamation and expectation.
The flesh profits nothing; Jesus' words about eating are spiritual, fulfilled by believing in him.
Coming to and believing in Christ is what it means to eat and drink him, so John 6 is about faith, not the Supper.
It is the Lord's Passover uses is for represents; the Supper replaces the Passover and uses the same figure.
Christ's single offering has perfected believers forever, so no sacrifice or physical reception is needed.

arguments.text: Jesus regularly uses metaphors with is (the door, the vine, the light), and Scripture names signs by what they represent, so a figurative is at the Supper is natural.
Jesus was physically present holding the bread when he said This is my body, so the disciples could not have understood the bread literally to be his body.
The ascension and session at God's right hand locate Christ's body in heaven until his return; his return will be visible, not hidden in elements.

Some early writers (for example Tertullian, *Against Marcion* 4.40, calling the bread a figure of the body) used figurative language, showing that symbolic readings have early roots, though how representative this is remains debated.

critiques.text: The memorial view breaks with the unanimous realism of the early church and empties Jesus' insistence in John 6 that his flesh is true food.
Reducing the Eucharist to human remembrance makes it our act rather than Christ's gift and loses its participation in the kingdom.
Turning is into signifies sets reason over the plain word; the Supper is Christ's testament, whose words must be taken as written.
Bare memorialism neglects Paul's language of participation; the Supper is not only our remembering Christ but God giving Christ to us.

responses.text: Memorialists reply that John 6 was spoken before the Supper existed and interprets eating as believing (v. 35, 47). Early writers used realist and figurative language side by side, so patristic unanimity is overstated.
Biblical remembrance is covenantal and active, and the Supper also looks forward to the kingdom (until he comes); this is not mere human recollection.
Taking Scripture plainly includes recognizing its figures; Luther himself read the cup is the new covenant as metonymy.
Many memorialists accept that Christ is spiritually present among his gathered people and that participation (koinonia) means fellowship in his benefits and with one another.

strawMen.strawMan: Zwingli and memorialists think the Supper is an empty ritual.
strawMen.correction: Zwingli spoke of Christ being present to the contemplation of faith, and memorialists see the Supper as a solemn act of remembrance, proclamation, fellowship and renewal, commanded by Christ.

strawMen.strawMan: The memorial view denies Christ's presence altogether.
strawMen.correction: It denies a bodily presence in or with the elements, but affirms Christ's presence by his Spirit among his people.

positive: Guards against superstition and idolatry of the elements.
Emphasizes faith, remembrance and the once-for-all cross.
Simple, accessible practice open to frequent and informal celebration.
negative: Can reduce the Supper to an infrequent add-on.
Critics say it loses the patristic and Reformational sense of the Supper as a means of grace.
The Marburg failure fractured Protestant unity.

adherents: Many Pentecostal and nondenominational evangelical churches
