This bread is my body: bread and body are given together in sacramental union.
Sacramental speech: the sign is called by the name of what it truly conveys to faith by the Spirit.
Is means signifies; the bread represents the body given on the cross.
A direct reference to eating Christ's real flesh in the Eucharist.
Eucharistic participation in the life-giving flesh of the incarnate Word.
Primarily spiritual eating by faith, which Lutherans distinguish from but connect to the oral eating in the Supper.
Feeding on Christ by faith through the Spirit, which the Supper especially seals.
A metaphor for believing in Christ, spoken before the Supper was instituted.
Participation in Christ's body and blood truly present after consecration.
Communion in the changed gifts that makes the church one body.
The bread we break is the means of participating in the body, so bread and body are united.
Real communion with Christ effected by the Spirit through the signs.
Fellowship in the benefits of Christ's death and with one another.
Unworthy reception profanes the body truly present.
Approaching the holy mysteries without repentance brings judgment.
Even the unworthy receive the body, but to their judgment.
The unworthy despise the body offered and are guilty of contempt, though they receive only signs.

Anamnesis makes the sacrifice present; do this commissions the apostles as priests.
Remembrance is liturgical participation in the saving events and the kingdom.
Given for you highlights the Supper as gift and forgiveness.
Remembrance is accompanied by the Spirit's real communication of Christ.
Remembrance is the defining purpose of the meal.
Christ's natural mode of presence is in heaven; his sacramental presence is of a different order.
The ascended Christ fills all things and is present in his mysteries.
Heaven is God's rule, not a container; it does not limit Christ's presence where promised.
Christ's body is in heaven, so believers are lifted to him by the Spirit.
Christ's body is in heaven until his return, so it is not in the elements.

Jesus often speaks in figures with is.
The cup and bread are a participation, not only a reminder.
Defining the mode at all rationalizes a mystery.
Koinonia means fellowship in Christ's benefits and with one another.

title: Creation, Genesis 1 and the Age of the Earth
question: How should Genesis 1–2 be read, and how does it relate to scientific accounts of the age of the earth and the history of life?
intro:
Genesis opens with God creating the heavens and the earth in six days and resting on the seventh. Christians agree that God is the sole Creator, that creation is good, and that humans bear his image. They disagree on what kind of text Genesis 1 is, what the days are, how old the earth is, and whether biological evolution is compatible with Scripture.

The debate is older than modern science. Augustine's *Literal Meaning of Genesis* (written c. 401–415) argued that the days need not be ordinary days and warned Christians against making confident claims about nature that unbelievers could see were false, since that would bring Scripture into disrepute (1.19). This entry presents five contemporary positions at equal depth: young-earth creationism, old-earth day-age creationism, the framework hypothesis, evolutionary creation, and the cosmic temple (functional) reading.

positions.name: Young-earth creationism
positions.summary:
Young-earth creationists read the days of Genesis 1 as six consecutive ordinary (approximately 24-hour) days, and the genealogies of Gen 5 and 11 as giving a largely continuous chronology, yielding an earth roughly six to ten thousand years old. Noah's flood was global and laid down much of the geological record. Animal death and suffering entered the world only after Adam's sin.

Adherents see this as the plain, historical reading of Genesis affirmed by Jesus and the apostles, and believe that scientific data, properly interpreted from biblical presuppositions, are consistent with it. Mainstream dating methods, they argue, rest on uniformitarian assumptions that a recent creation and a global flood would overturn. The view has older roots (for example Ussher's chronology) but took its modern form with *The Genesis Flood* (1961).

figures.name: Henry M. Morris and John C. Whitcomb
figures.profession: Hydraulic engineer and Old Testament theologian
figures.bio: Together they wrote the founding text of modern young-earth creationism, arguing that a global flood explains the geological column. Morris later founded the Institute for Creation Research (1970).

figures.name: Ken Ham
figures.profession: Australian-born Christian apologist, founder of Answers in Genesis
figures.bio: Founded Answers in Genesis in the United States in 1994, and led the building of the Creation Museum (2007) and Ark Encounter (2016) in Kentucky. He is the most prominent popular advocate of young-earth creationism.

works.author: Ken Ham
works.title: The Lie: Evolution

figures.name: James Ussher
figures.profession: Church of Ireland Archbishop of Armagh and scholar
figures.bio: Constructed a detailed world chronology dating creation to 4004 BC, which was printed in the margins of many English Bibles and became the classic expression of a young-earth timeline before modern geology.

works.author: James Ussher
works.title: Annales Veteris Testamenti

positions.context: Before the nineteenth century most Christians assumed a young earth, though not uniformly a literal week (Augustine favored instantaneous creation). The rise of geology led many evangelicals to accept an old earth by 1900. George McCready Price's flood geology (1923) was largely ignored until Whitcomb and Morris revived it in 1961, amid Cold War science education debates. Young-earth creationism then grew rapidly through organizations such as the Institute for Creation Research and Answers in Genesis, and remains widespread among American evangelicals.
claims: The days of Genesis 1 are ordinary consecutive days.
The earth and universe are thousands, not billions, of years old.
Noah's flood was global and produced much of the fossil record.
There was no animal death or suffering before the fall.
Adam and Eve were specially created as the first humans, from whom all humans descend.

scriptures.reading: Evening and morning with a numbered day signal an ordinary day.
The Sabbath command bases the human week on God's six days of creation, implying days of the same kind.
Jesus says God made them male and female from the beginning of creation, not billions of years later.
Death entered the world through one man's sin, ruling out death before Adam.
Creation was subjected to futility because of the fall and groans awaiting redemption.
All the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered, indicating a global flood.
Peter treats the flood as a world-destroying judgment, parallel to the coming judgment.

arguments.text: Hebrew yom with a number and with evening and morning elsewhere refers to ordinary days, and Exodus explicitly links creation days to the work week.
If death, disease and predation existed for millions of years before Adam, God called a world full of suffering very good, and the link between sin and death in the gospel is weakened.
Most Jewish and Christian interpreters before the modern period assumed a young earth, so the old-earth readings arose under pressure from science rather than from the text.
The genealogies of Gen 5 and 11 give ages at fatherhood, forming a chronology with no obvious room for vast gaps.

critiques.text: The physical evidence for an old universe, from starlight distance to radiometric dating, is overwhelming and consistent; God's general revelation in nature cannot contradict his word.
Genesis 1 has a carefully patterned literary structure, with the sun created on day four, which signals a non-chronological, topical arrangement rather than a sequential stopwatch.
Flood geology contradicts virtually all of modern geology, biology and physics; requiring it as a test of orthodoxy places a needless stumbling block before scientists.
The view reads Genesis as answering modern material questions about age and process, which ancient readers were not asking; the text is about functions and God's rest in his temple.

responses.text: Young-earth scientists argue that the data are interpreted through assumptions, and they offer alternative models (for example different starlight models and accelerated decay). Nature is general revelation, but scientific interpretations of it are fallible human work.
The structure of Genesis 1 does not exclude chronology; the text uses the narrative sequence form and numbered days, and Exod 20:11 treats them as a sequence.
They answer that the Bible is the final authority, and that history shows scientific consensus changes; a global flood would itself overturn the uniformitarian assumptions behind standard geology.
Genesis 1 certainly portrays God's ordering and rest, but the text also describes material things being made (bara, asah) on specific days.

strawMen.strawMan: Young-earth creationists reject all science.
strawMen.correction: They accept operational science and many have advanced degrees; they dispute specific historical interpretations of data and assumptions about the past.

strawMen.strawMan: Young-earth creationism teaches that no species ever changes.
strawMen.correction: Most young-earth creationists accept substantial variation and speciation within created kinds; they deny universal common descent.

positive: Upholds a strong view of the historical character of Genesis.
Links the gospel tightly to the fall and to a coming restored creation.
Engaged lay Christians widely in questions of science and faith.
negative: Critics note it can set Christian young people against scientific careers.
Has caused division and suspicion within evangelical institutions.
Can make Christianity appear anti-intellectual to outsiders.

adherents: Answers in Genesis and Institute for Creation Research
Many Baptist, Pentecostal and nondenominational evangelical churches

positions.name: Old-earth day-age creationism
positions.summary:
Day-age creationists hold that the days of Genesis 1 are long, sequential periods of time, and that the order of events in Genesis broadly matches the order established by science. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old and the earth about 4.5 billion, consistent with mainstream cosmology and geology.

They nevertheless reject universal common descent. God intervened supernaturally at key points to create new kinds of life and especially to create Adam and Eve, the historical first humans. Hugh Ross and Reasons to Believe pursue a concordist method, testing Scripture and science against each other in a testable creation model, and see the Big Bang as strong evidence for a transcendent Creator.

figures.name: Hugh Miller
figures.profession: Scottish geologist, writer and Free Church layman
figures.bio: A self-taught geologist and evangelical who popularized reading the creation days as geological ages, arguing that Genesis describes in visionary form the great epochs revealed by the rocks.

works.author: Hugh Miller
works.title: The Testimony of the Rocks

figures.name: Hugh Ross
figures.profession: Canadian astrophysicist and apologist
figures.bio: Founded Reasons to Believe in 1986 to show the agreement of science and Scripture. He argues that Genesis 1 accurately describes cosmic and earth history from the viewpoint of an observer on the earth's surface.

works.author: Hugh Ross
works.title: The Genesis Question

works.author: Hugh Ross
works.title: A Matter of Days: Resolving a Creation Controversy

figures.name: Gleason L. Archer
figures.profession: Old Testament scholar at Trinity Evangelical Divinity School
figures.bio: A defender of inerrancy who argued exegetically for long creation days, and later co-wrote the day-age contribution to a major multi-view volume with Ross.

works.author: Hugh Ross and Gleason L. Archer
works.title: The Day-Age View, in The Genesis Debate (ed. David G. Hagopian)

positions.context: As geology established the earth's great age in the early nineteenth century, many evangelicals adopted either the gap theory (popularized by Thomas Chalmers and later the Scofield Bible) or the day-age view (Hugh Miller, Arnold Guyot, James Dana). Leading conservatives of the early twentieth century, including several writers of *The Fundamentals* and William Jennings Bryan at the 1925 Scopes trial, accepted long ages. After 1961 young-earth views spread, and Reasons to Believe (1986) revived day-age concordism as a scientific apologetic.
claims: The days of Genesis 1 are long, sequential periods.
The universe and earth are billions of years old, as science indicates.
God supernaturally created new kinds of life at intervals; universal common descent is rejected.
Adam and Eve were specially created as the first humans, relatively recently.
Nature and Scripture are two harmonious revelations, and their agreement can be tested.

scriptures.reading: In the day that the Lord God made the earth and heavens uses day for the whole creation period, showing yom can mean an extended time.
The seventh day has no evening and morning, suggesting God's rest continues; if day seven is long, the others can be too.
God's Sabbath rest remains open to believers, confirming the seventh day is an ongoing era.
A thousand years are like a day to God; divine days need not be human days.
The heavens declare God's glory; nature's testimony is reliable revelation.
God's power is clearly seen in what has been made, so scientific evidence is a valid witness.

arguments.text: Too many events occur on day six (naming animals, Adam's search for a partner, Eve's creation) for an ordinary day.
God does not deceive; if the universe appears billions of years old by multiple independent methods, it is billions of years old.
Several church fathers (Augustine, and with different reasoning Origen and others) did not read the days as ordinary days, so non-literal days are not merely a modern compromise.
Hebrew has no more specific word for a long era than yom, and it is used flexibly elsewhere for extended periods.

critiques.text: Day-age accepts death and suffering long before the fall and bends the plain meaning of numbered days with evening and morning to fit secular science.
Concordism forces the text to match modern science and the order does not fit well (birds before land animals, plants before the sun).
Rejecting common descent while accepting the rest of mainstream science is inconsistent; the genetic evidence for common ancestry is as strong as the evidence for the earth's age.
Reading Genesis as a scientific account of cosmic history imposes modern questions on an ancient text; it is about functions, not material chronology.

responses.text: Ross argues Rom 5 concerns human spiritual death, and that Scripture praises God for predators and their prey, so animal death is not inherently evil.
Day-age proponents argue that, read from the earth's surface, day four is when the sun became visible through a clearing atmosphere, and the sequence fits closely.
They see real scientific gaps in evolutionary mechanisms, especially for the origin of life and major transitions, which fits episodic creation.
Genesis is ancient and functional, but it also asserts real events; God's word speaks truly about the world, which leaves room for testing it against discoveries.

strawMen.strawMan: Old-earth creationists accept evolution.
strawMen.correction: Day-age creationists reject universal common descent and argue for repeated special creation, including the special creation of Adam and Eve.

strawMen.strawMan: Day-age creationists do not take Genesis literally.
strawMen.correction: They argue that their reading is the literal one, since yom literally can mean a long period; they also affirm a historical Adam and historical fall.

positive: Encourages science-friendly evangelical apologetics.
Affirms both a historical Adam and mainstream cosmology.
Uses cosmology (fine-tuning, the beginning of the universe) as evidence for God.
negative: Criticized by young-earth and evolutionary creationists alike.
Concordist claims can be overturned by new science.
Can make biblical interpretation dependent on current scientific models.

positions.name: Framework hypothesis
positions.summary:
The framework hypothesis reads the seven days of Genesis 1 as a literary framework, not a chronological sequence. The days form two parallel triads: days one to three create realms (light and darkness; sky and seas; land and plants), and days four to six fill them with rulers or inhabitants (lights; birds and fish; land animals and humans). Day seven, God's Sabbath, crowns the whole.

The days are real days in the imagery of the narrative, a work week used as a picture, but the picture is not intended to tell us the order or length of creation. Genesis 1 is therefore silent on the age of the earth. Most framework advocates affirm the historicity of Adam and the fall, and the view is held by many confessional Reformed scholars who otherwise hold high views of Scripture.

figures.name: Arie Noordtzij
figures.profession: Old Testament professor at Utrecht
figures.bio: Dutch Reformed scholar usually credited with first proposing that the days of Genesis 1 form a literary framework rather than a chronology.

figures.profession: Old Testament scholar at Westminster and Gordon-Conwell seminaries
figures.bio: Developed the most influential exegetical defense of the framework view, arguing from Gen 2:5 that ordinary providence operated during creation, and from a two-register cosmology in which the creation week is an upper-register picture.

works.title: Because It Had Not Rained, Westminster Theological Journal 20

works.author: Meredith G. Kline
works.title: Space and Time in the Genesis Cosmogony, Perspectives on Science and Christian Faith 48

figures.profession: French Reformed Baptist theologian at the Faculté libre de théologie évangélique, Vaux-sur-Seine
figures.bio: Offered a careful literary reading of Gen 1–3, presenting the framework as the most natural interpretation of the text's structure while affirming the historicity of the fall.

works.author: Henri Blocher
works.title: In the Beginning: The Opening Chapters of Genesis

positions.context: Noordtzij proposed the view in the Netherlands in 1924; Nicolaas Ridderbos and others developed it. Kline introduced it to American Reformed circles from 1958. In the 1990s it became controversial in the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church; the PCA's 2000 report on creation days judged it, among others, an acceptable view within its confessional bounds, while some presbyteries disagreed.
claims: The seven days are a literary framework rather than a chronological sequence.
Days one to three (realms) correspond to days four to six (rulers or inhabitants).
The text teaches theology (God's sovereign creation and Sabbath rest), not the age or sequence of creation.
God's ordinary providence was operating during creation, as Gen 2:5 implies.
Genesis 1 is compatible with various scientific accounts of origins, while Adam and the fall remain historical.

scriptures.reading: Formless and empty sets up the two problems solved in the two triads: forming realms and filling them.
Lights on day four correspond to light on day one, a topical rather than chronological arrangement.
No plants had sprung up because God had not caused it to rain, implying ordinary providence was operating, not miraculously compressed timescales.
Human work-and-rest is patterned on God's, by analogy rather than identity of days.
God's seventh-day rest is unending, showing the days function in a different register from human days.
Heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool: Scripture uses an upper and lower register cosmology.

arguments.text: The parallelism of days one to three with four to six is too deliberate to ignore, and the creation of light before the sun is best explained by topical arrangement.
Gen 2:5-6 explains the absence of plants by the lack of rain and of a man to work the ground, an ordinary-providence explanation that assumes normal, not miraculously accelerated, processes.
Since the seventh day is clearly not an ordinary 24-hour day, the days function analogically, and analogies need not specify duration or sequence.
Ancient Near Eastern texts often used seven-day patterns for completed construction (for example temple dedications), suggesting a literary convention.

critiques.text: The narrative uses the Hebrew sequential verb form and numbered days, marks of historical narrative; the framework view is driven by a desire to avoid conflict with old-earth science.
By making Genesis silent on chronology, the framework view gives up the opportunity to show that Genesis accurately anticipates science.
Framework advocates often stop short of accepting the scientific implications, such as common descent, that their literary reading would allow.
The literary pattern is real, but its purpose is cosmic temple inauguration; framework advocates sometimes miss the functional and temple focus.

responses.text: Narrative form does not determine whether a sequence is chronological; Kline and Blocher argue from the internal evidence of the text, and Noordtzij's proposal arose from exegesis rather than apologetic pressure.
Framework advocates value general revelation but think Genesis 1 was never intended to be compared with modern science, so concordism risks distorting it.
Framework is a reading of Genesis 1 only; it leaves scientific questions open and does not decide questions about Adam addressed by Gen 2–3 and Rom 5.
Kline himself emphasized the cosmos as God's royal temple; framework and temple readings are largely compatible.

strawMen.strawMan: The framework hypothesis says Genesis 1 is myth or fiction.
strawMen.correction: It treats Genesis 1 as true revelation about real creation, using a literary framework; most proponents hold a high view of inspiration.

strawMen.strawMan: Framework advocates accept evolution.
strawMen.correction: The view is neutral on mechanisms; many framework advocates reject universal common descent and affirm the special creation of Adam.

positive: Draws attention to Genesis 1's careful literary artistry.
Allows confessional churches to hold different views of the age of the earth.
Emphasizes Sabbath and theological meaning.
negative: Perceived by critics as a sophisticated way of evading the text.
Has caused controversy in some Presbyterian denominations.
Can appear abstract to lay readers.

positions.name: Evolutionary creation (theistic evolution)
positions.summary:
Evolutionary creationists affirm that God created the universe and all life, and that he did so through processes science describes: a 13.8-billion-year-old universe and the evolution of all life, including humans, from common ancestors. God's ordinary providence sustains these processes, so evolution is not an alternative to creation but its means.

On this view Genesis 1–11 communicates theological truth through ancient cosmological categories that should not be read as scientific claims. Evolutionary creationists differ on Adam and Eve: some see them as historical representatives or a pair within an early population, others read Adam as an archetype or figure. All affirm the reality of sin, the need for redemption, and the resurrection of Christ.

figures.name: Asa Gray
figures.profession: Harvard botanist and Presbyterian
figures.bio: Darwin's leading American supporter, who argued that natural selection was compatible with design and divine providence.

works.author: Asa Gray
works.title: Darwiniana

figures.name: Francis S. Collins
figures.profession: Geneticist, director of the Human Genome Project and later of the US National Institutes of Health
figures.bio: An evangelical Christian who argued that genome data strongly confirm common ancestry and that faith and evolution are compatible. He founded the BioLogos Foundation in 2007.

works.title: The Language of God: A Scientist Presents Evidence for Belief

figures.name: Denis O. Lamoureux
figures.profession: Canadian theologian and biologist at St Joseph's College, University of Alberta
figures.bio: Holds doctorates in theology and biology. He argues that Scripture accommodates an ancient science of the day, and that Adam was not a historical person, while holding to evangelical faith.

works.author: Denis O. Lamoureux
works.title: Evolutionary Creation: A Christian Approach to Evolution

positions.context: After Darwin's *Origin of Species* (1859), many Christian thinkers, including some conservatives such as B. B. Warfield and James Orr, were open to forms of evolution under providence. Twentieth-century fundamentalism hardened opposition, especially after the Scopes trial (1925). Catholic teaching (Pius XII, *Humani generis*, 1950; John Paul II, 1996) cautiously allowed evolution of the human body while affirming the special creation of the soul. Collins's book and BioLogos, launched in 2009 after founding in 2007, gave the view a prominent evangelical voice.
claims: God created everything, and he used evolutionary processes as his means.
The universe and earth are billions of years old, and all life shares common ancestry.
Genesis 1–11 uses ancient categories to teach theology, not science.
Humans are uniquely made in God's image, whatever their biological origins.
Sin, the fall and redemption in Christ are real, though views of a historical Adam vary.

scriptures.reading: Let the earth bring forth living creatures: creation involves God working through natural processes.
God knits each person in the womb, an ordinary biological process, so natural means can be divine creation.
All things are created through Christ and hold together in him; natural processes are his sustaining work.
The firmament reflects ancient cosmology, showing God accommodated his message to ancient science.
Poetic creation imagery shows Scripture uses figures to speak about nature.
God's ongoing providential work in nature, including predators and life cycles, is called his creating.

arguments.text: Shared genetic features, such as broken genes and retroviral insertions in the same locations in humans and apes, are best explained by common ancestry.
Scripture describes the sky as a solid firmament with waters above it, ancient science God did not correct; so he likewise did not teach modern biology.

Augustine warned against embarrassing the faith with claims about nature contrary to evident knowledge (*Literal Meaning of Genesis* 1.19), and Galileo's case shows the cost of reading science into Scripture.
God's providential use of natural causes, such as rain, growth and birth, is consistently called his own work, so evolution can be too.

critiques.text: Evolution requires billions of years of death before the fall and makes Adam either non-historical or not the ancestor of all, undermining Paul's gospel.
Evolutionary mechanisms cannot account for the origin of life and major biological innovations; God intervened in history.
Framework advocates who are open to evolution still insist that the historicity of Adam and the fall is essential to the gospel; some evolutionary creationists give it up.
Evolutionary creationists sometimes simply exchange one concordism for another; Genesis is not about mechanisms at all, so it neither endorses nor rules out evolution.

responses.text: Many evolutionary creationists say Paul is speaking of spiritual death and alienation from God, and some hold to a historical Adam as a representative head of an early human population.
They caution that gap-based arguments shrink as science advances, and that God's working through natural laws is still his work.
BioLogos hosts a range of views on Adam, including historical ones, and treats the historical Adam question as an open conversation rather than a settled denial.
Evolutionary creationists largely agree; they accept evolution on scientific grounds and use readings like Walton's to show Genesis does not conflict with it.

strawMen.strawMan: Theistic evolutionists believe God is unnecessary because evolution explains everything.
strawMen.correction: Evolutionary creationists hold that God created and sustains all natural processes; science describes his customary ways of working.

strawMen.strawMan: Evolutionary creationists deny miracles.
strawMen.correction: They affirm miracles, including the incarnation and the bodily resurrection of Jesus, while holding that biological history did not require them.

positive: Removes a stumbling block for scientists and students considering faith.
Encourages Christian engagement in mainstream science.
Highlights God's ongoing providence over nature.
negative: Raises difficult questions about Adam, the fall and original sin.
Critics say it concedes too much to naturalism.
Has provoked controversy and dismissals in some evangelical institutions.

adherents: Many Catholic and mainline Protestant scientists and theologians

positions.name: Cosmic temple (functional) reading
positions.summary:
John Walton argues that Genesis 1 must be read as ancient Near Eastern cosmology. In the ancient world, to create something meant mainly to give it a function and role in an ordered system, not to manufacture its material. Genesis 1 describes God assigning functions to the cosmos over seven days in order to make it his temple, and on the seventh day he rests, meaning he takes up residence and begins to rule from it.

The seven days are real days, but they are days of inauguration of a cosmic temple, not days of material origins. Genesis 1 therefore makes no claims about the age of the earth or the processes of material origins. Walton is open to science on those questions, and in later work suggests Adam and Eve were historical persons chosen as archetypal priestly representatives rather than necessarily the biological ancestors of all humans.

figures.profession: Old Testament scholar at Wheaton College
figures.bio: Specialist in the Old Testament and ancient Near East who popularized the functional, temple reading of Genesis 1 through a series of accessible Lost World books.

works.title: The Temple and the Church's Mission

figures.profession: Jewish biblical scholar at Harvard Divinity School

works.author: Jon D. Levenson
works.title: Creation and the Persistence of Evil

positions.context: Temple readings of Genesis 1 emerged from twentieth-century study of ancient Near Eastern creation and temple-building texts and from biblical theology. Walton's 2009 book popularized the idea for evangelical readers during intense debate over evolution and Adam, offering a way to take Genesis literally in its ancient sense while setting aside conflict with modern science.
claims: Genesis 1 should be read in its ancient Near Eastern context.
Creation in Genesis 1 is primarily about assigning functions, not making material.
The seven days are the inauguration of the cosmos as God's temple; his rest is enthronement.
Genesis 1 does not address the age of the earth or material origins, so it is compatible with science.
Adam and Eve are archetypal representatives, and possibly historical persons.

scriptures.reading: God's rest is not inactivity but taking up residence and rule, as in temple dedications.
God's resting place is his temple; rest language belongs to divine enthronement.
Zion is God's resting place forever where he dwells, confirming rest equals dwelling.
Heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool; the cosmos is God's temple.
Formless and empty describes a nonfunctional state, not absence of matter.
The lights are described by their functions (signs, seasons, days and years), not their physical make-up.

arguments.text: Ancient Near Eastern cosmologies, Egyptian and Mesopotamian, focus on naming, ordering and functions, and connect creation with temple-building and divine rest.
Genesis 1 describes the sun, moon and stars by function rather than material structure, and the climax is God's rest, consistent with temple inauguration.
If the text was written for ancient Israelites, its meaning must be what they could understand; modern questions about age and mechanism were not in view.
Eden and the tabernacle share features (cherubim, eastward entrance, gold and onyx, priestly work and keep), suggesting Eden is a sanctuary.

critiques.text: Walton's material-functional distinction is a false dichotomy; Genesis describes material things being made, and Exodus 20:11 says God made heaven and earth in six days.
If Genesis says nothing about material origins, it gives no positive testimony to a Creator of matter, weakening apologetics; Heb 11:3 is about material origin.
Framework advocates share the temple emphasis but argue that Walton's functional-only claim is overstated; the literary structure, not ancient parallels alone, should govern interpretation.
Some evolutionary creationists, such as Lamoureux, think Scripture does make ancient material-scientific claims (the firmament), and that Walton underplays accommodation.

responses.text: Walton grants God is the material Creator, affirmed elsewhere in Scripture; his claim is that Genesis 1 specifically is about functional origins, and verbs like bara are always used of God's ordering activity.
Material creation by God is taught elsewhere, and Genesis 1 offers a powerful theological account of God's purposes and presence in the world.
Walton builds his case from both the text's language and its ancient context, which he sees as complementary to literary analysis.
Walton accepts that Scripture reflects ancient cosmic geography but argues that the teaching point is functional, so accommodation does not undermine the text's authority.

strawMen.strawMan: Walton says God did not create the material universe.
strawMen.correction: Walton explicitly affirms that God created the material universe; he argues only that Genesis 1 is not focused on that question.

strawMen.strawMan: The cosmic temple view is a way of smuggling in evolution.
strawMen.correction: The view is a reading of Genesis based on ancient context; it is compatible with several scientific positions and is held by some who reject evolution.

positive: Draws attention to the temple and worship themes of creation.
Encourages reading Scripture in its ancient context.
Offers a way out of science-versus-Bible conflict for many students.
negative: Critics argue it makes Genesis inaccessible without specialist knowledge.
The functional-only claim is contested by many Hebrew scholars.
Leaves questions about Adam and the fall unresolved for some.

Some temple-theology readers in Reformed circles

title: Inspiration and Inerrancy of Scripture
question: In what sense is the Bible inspired by God, and does inspiration guarantee that Scripture is without error in everything it affirms, or in matters of faith and salvation?
intro:
Christians of every tradition confess that Scripture is inspired by God, echoing 2 Tim 3:16, where all Scripture is described as God-breathed. They disagree about what inspiration guarantees. Is every statement, including history and science, free from error? Is the Bible infallible in what it teaches about salvation and conduct, while reflecting the limitations of its human authors elsewhere? How should the Bible's human, culturally embedded character be understood?

Augustine wrote to Jerome that if he found something in Scripture that seemed contrary to truth, he would assume a faulty manuscript, a mistaken translation or his own misunderstanding (Letter 82). Modern debate intensified with historical criticism in the nineteenth century. This entry presents four positions at equal depth: strict inerrancy, limited inerrancy or infallibility, the incarnational model, and the Catholic teaching of *Dei Verbum* with its debated interpretations.

positions.name: Strict (full) inerrancy
positions.summary:
Strict inerrancy holds that Scripture, being breathed out by God, is without error in all that it affirms, whether about God, salvation, history or the natural world. Inspiration is verbal (extending to the words) and plenary (extending to all parts), and it applies strictly to the original autographs, though faithful copies and translations carry the authority of the originals to the extent they reproduce them.

Inerrancy does not mean a mechanical dictation theory, nor that every text must be read literally. It allows for phenomenological language, round numbers, free quotation, varied literary genres and the authors' own styles. Apparent discrepancies are to be harmonized where possible, and otherwise left unresolved in confidence that God's word is true. The 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy is the classic modern expression.

Inerrantists affirm the value of the church's interpretive tradition, but hold that Scripture alone is the final infallible rule over every tradition.

positions.name: Limited inerrancy or infallibility
positions.summary:
This position holds that Scripture is fully inspired and infallible, or inerrant, in all that it intends to teach about God, salvation, faith and practice, but that inspiration does not guarantee accuracy in incidental matters of science, chronology or historical detail that are not part of its teaching purpose. The Bible accomplishes infallibly the purpose for which God gave it.

Proponents, many of them evangelicals, argue that this is the historic view of the church before the Princeton theologians made inerrancy a matter of precise factual accuracy. They stress the Bible's purpose, the importance of not resting faith on harmonization of every detail, and the freedom of scholars to follow evidence. Critics, beginning with Harold Lindsell, saw this as a slippery slope toward liberalism.

Proponents note that many Catholic scholars read Dei Verbum 11 the same way, and that the debate within Catholicism shows the question is open.

positions.name: Incarnational model
positions.summary:
The incarnational model draws an analogy between Scripture and Christ: as Christ is fully divine and fully human, so the Bible is fully God's word and fully human words, shaped by the cultures, genres and limitations of its ancient authors. The Bible's ancient Near Eastern parallels, its theological diversity, and the apostles' creative use of the Old Testament are not problems to explain away but evidence of how God chose to speak.

Proponents argue that evangelical doctrines of Scripture should be built inductively from what the Bible is actually like, rather than deductively from what an inspired book must be. Peter Enns, the leading advocate, argues that once we accept God's willingness to accommodate himself to ancient human ways of thinking, many tensions disappear. The analogy itself is old, used by Herman Bavinck and by the Catholic *Dei Verbum* 13, though Enns and others push it further.

The model holds that Scripture reliably testifies to God's acts climaxing in Christ, and that this is what it is given to do.

positions.name: Catholic teaching: Dei Verbum
positions.summary:
The Second Vatican Council's Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, *Dei Verbum* (1965), teaches that God is the author of Scripture, having chosen human authors who were true authors using their own faculties. Because what the inspired authors assert is asserted by the Holy Spirit, the books of Scripture teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth that God wanted put into the sacred writings for the sake of our salvation (DV 11). Scripture is read within the living Tradition and interpreted authoritatively by the Magisterium (DV 10).

The interpretation of the phrase for the sake of our salvation is debated. A restrictive reading, associated with scholars such as Raymond Brown, holds that inerrancy covers saving truth, leaving room for error in incidental matters. A comprehensive reading, associated with Cardinal Augustin Bea and others, holds that the phrase states the purpose of Scripture, not a limit on its truth, consistent with earlier encyclicals such as *Providentissimus Deus* (1893). The Pontifical Biblical Commission's 2014 document explored the question without fully settling it.

positions.context: Catholic teaching on inspiration was shaped by the Council of Trent (1546) and the First Vatican Council (1870), which taught that God is the author of Scripture. Leo XIII's *Providentissimus Deus* (1893) affirmed that inspiration excludes all error. Pius XII's *Divino Afflante Spiritu* (1943) encouraged attention to literary genres. Dei Verbum (1965) synthesized these. The phrase for the sake of our salvation was added in the final drafting, and its meaning has been debated since.

Scripture teaches firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God willed for our salvation.
Scripture must be interpreted with attention to literary genres and in the light of Tradition and the Magisterium.
Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source.
The incarnational analogy illuminates Scripture's human form (DV 13).

arguments.text: Dei Verbum stands in continuity with Augustine, Trent, Vatican I and the encyclicals, all of which affirmed Scripture's freedom from error, while the comprehensive reading holds that DV 11 changed emphasis rather than doctrine.
Scripture presents itself as given for salvation, and the church as its interpreter.

critiques.text: Protestant inerrantists welcome DV's affirmation of truth without error but reject the role of Tradition and Magisterium as co-authorities, and worry that the restrictive reading has prevailed in Catholic scholarship.
Proponents of limited inerrancy find DV 11 supportive, but argue that Catholic appeals to Magisterium cannot settle historical questions.
Incarnational proponents appreciate DV 13 but find the Magisterium's oversight potentially restrictive of honest historical scholarship.

responses.text: Catholics reply that Tradition and Magisterium do not stand above Scripture but serve it, as DV 10 states, and that the canon itself was recognized by the church.
The Magisterium does not decide historical questions by fiat but guards faith, and Catholic scholars enjoy freedom in historical study within it.
Since Divino Afflante Spiritu the Church has encouraged critical scholarship, holding that faith and reason are not opposed.

argumentMap.text: Scripture is without error in all that it affirms.
God cannot lie, and Scripture is God-breathed.
Jesus treated Scripture's details as reliable.
Scripture's stated purpose is salvation, not precision in every detail.
Saving truths depend on historical events, so history cannot be detached.
Scripture is infallible in its saving purpose.
These are written that you may believe.
Distinguishing saving from incidental matters is arbitrary.
Scripture is fully divine and fully human, like Christ.
The Word became flesh.
God spoke in many ways through human writers.
Christ's humanity was without sin, so Scripture's humanity should be without error.
Sinlessness is not omniscience; Jesus grew in wisdom.
Scripture teaches without error the truth God willed for our salvation.
The Church is the pillar and bulwark of truth.
Tradition must not override the word of God.
The Magisterium is not above the word of God but serves it (DV 10).
The phrase for the sake of salvation limits inerrancy's scope.
